items.title: Maslow's pyramid was never drawn by Maslow
items.claim: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs is taught with a pyramid. What did Maslow himself draw?

options.text: He drew the pyramid himself in his 1943 paper
He never drew it as a pyramid; the pyramid representation was introduced by management consultants and textbooks in the 1960s
He drew it as a circle to indicate non-linear progression
He explicitly rejected any visual representation

items.reveal:
Todd Bridgman, Stephen Cummings and John Ballard's 2019 paper in the Academy of Management Learning & Education traced the pyramid to Charles McDermid's 1960 management article in Business Horizons. Maslow's 1943 'A Theory of Human Motivation' described needs as overlapping and dynamic — not rigidly tiered.

Maslow himself, late in his career, qualified the theory heavily: needs can be pursued in parallel, prioritisation varies by culture and individual, and self-actualisation isn't a 'top' level so much as a developmental orientation.

Empirical tests find weak support for the strict hierarchy.
items.why: The most-taught motivation diagram in business education was drawn by someone other than the named theorist and oversimplifies what he wrote. Worth checking what's in the textbook against what's in the source.

items.title: Most mergers and acquisitions destroy shareholder value
items.claim: Multiple long-run studies of M&A outcomes (KPMG, Bain, Harvard Business Review reviews) report what share of deals fail to create value for the acquiring firm's shareholders?
items.reveal:
KPMG's recurring M&A studies, Bain & Company's analyses, and Roger Martin's 2016 HBR piece 'M&A: The One Thing You Need to Get Right' all converge: 70-90% of acquisitions fail to deliver the anticipated synergies, often because the acquirer overpays.

Specific failures: AOL-Time Warner (2000, $165bn), Daimler-Chrysler (1998), Quaker-Snapple (1994), Microsoft-Nokia (2014). The 'winner's curse' (Thaler, 1988) explains why competitive bidding tends to produce winners who overestimated.

Organic growth tends to deliver more predictable returns but at a slower pace.
items.why: M&A is one of the most-used growth strategies and one of the worst-performing. The gap between expected and actual synergies is systematically positive.

items.title: SWOT analysis is often misused as a sorting exercise
items.claim: SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) emerged from Albert Humphrey's work at Stanford in the 1960s-70s. What's the standard critique?

options.text: It is a complete strategic plan
SWOT identifies factors but provides no method to translate them into strategy; without TOWS-style cross-pairing (S-O, S-T, W-O, W-T), it's just four bullet-point lists
It can only be used for new ventures

items.reveal:
Heinz Weihrich's 1982 TOWS matrix paired Strengths with Opportunities (offensive strategies), Strengths with Threats (defensive), Weaknesses with Opportunities (improvement), and Weaknesses with Threats (mitigation).

The core SWOT critique is that without this step, the framework lists factors without forcing a strategic choice. Most student SWOTs stop at the list stage — which is descriptive, not strategic.
items.why: SWOT looks like analysis but often delivers sorting. The strategic value is in the combinations across quadrants.
